title: Georgia man sues Flock, sheriff's office over alleged ALPR-fueled retaliation
gist: A Georgia business owner sued Flock and the Coweta County Sheriff's Office, alleging deputies ran repeated unjustified license plate searches on his car in retaliation for his earlier excessive-force suit. The complaint targets Flock's free-text search justification field, which Flock said in August 2026 it would replace with required case codes.

insights.claim: Tyler Murkerson alleges Coweta County deputies repeatedly searched his plate in Flock's system and followed or monitored him while his excessive-force lawsuit against the department was pending.
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: ALPR misuse litigation creates legal and reputational liability for both agencies and the vendor.

insights.claim: The complaint alleges Flock failed to prevent illegal surveillance by accepting free-text entries instead of specific case numbers; the only justifications entered for searches of Murkerson's car were 'info' and '37'.
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: Weak audit controls by design are the core vendor-liability theory; watch whether courts treat this as product negligence.
insights.quote: The only justifications entered for the searches of Mr. Murkerson’s vehicle were ‘info’ and ‘37.’

insights.claim: The plaintiff's attorneys argue the harm is warrantless Fourth Amendment-implicated searches without controls, rather than photographing license plates itself.
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: Legal framing focuses on search authorization, which could shape how ALPR use is regulated.

insights.claim: In August 2026 Flock announced it would require case codes for all law enforcement searches by year end, and the Coweta sheriff began an audit in which three employees resigned before completion.
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: Product changes concede the control gap and add compliance costs and friction for agency customers.

insights.claim: Hundreds of law enforcement agencies have recently dropped Flock, largely over a backlash against overbroad and unwanted surveillance.
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: Customer churn is a key risk to Flock's municipal contract base.
insights.locator: Flock has been under increased scrutiny

insights.claim: Secure Justice's Brian Hofer argues guardrails do not work because 'culture eats policy for lunch' and recommends prohibiting the technology until policing culture changes.
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: Advocates are pushing bans rather than policy fixes, raising the odds of local prohibitions.

insights.claim: Flock says it stands by its technology and intends to vigorously defend the suit.
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: Expect a contested case rather than a quick settlement.
